list.listitem: Screen high-risk patients for tuberculosis (TB). B
If a screen for TB is positive, patient needs a chest X-ray, and if pulmonary TB is suspected, 3 induced sputums. B
For latent TB, one of three 3-4 month regimens is recommended by CDC.A
Active TB should be treated with a 2-month initiation phase with 4 drugs and a 4- to 7-month continuation phase. A
Repeat sputum cultures at the end of the 2-month initiation phase. If the culture is positive, consider prolonging or changing treatment. B
Children with non-severe symptomatic TB can use a 4 month regimen of standard fixed dose anti-tubercular drugs. B

background.definition: Tuberculosis is an infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It is spread from person to person through droplets.

list.listitem: In 2004 there were 14,517 confirmed cases (4.9 cases per 100,000) in the United States.
53.7% of these cases were in foreign-born patients.
WHO estimates that each year more than 8 million new cases occur and approximately 3 million persons die from the disease.
TB has a large social impact. It occurs disproportionately among homeless, malnourished, and otherwise disadvantaged populations.
M. tuberculosis is a slow growing bacillus that can grow within alveolar macrophages.
Tubercle bacilli enter alveolar macrophages. The likelihood of transmission is associated with the length of time a person is exposed to the droplets and the immune status of the exposed individual.
If no host response occurs, the bacilli spread via the lymphatics to the hilar lymph nodes and then through the bloodstream to multiple sites.
High-risk patients should be screened for TB (). B

The USPSTF concludes there is adequate evidence that the benefits outweigh the risks of screening for latent tuberculosis infection in adults 18 years and older who are at increased risk for infection (B grade recommendation). B
Screening for TB may be performed with the tuberculin skin test (TST). C
The QuantiFeron-TB Gold test (QFT-G) can be used in place of TST especially in patients who do not have known exposure to TB and have had the bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccination. C

A RCT in Vietnam concluded that active community-wide screening in asymptomatic people using rapid nucleic acid amplification testing of spontaneously expectorated sputum samples was associated compared with standard passive case detectin alone, was associated with 41% fewer cases of culture confirmed pulmonary TB after 4 years of screening.
Screening for TB should be conducted only among groups at high risk (see ).

The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) concludes there is adequate evidence that the benefits outweigh the risks of screening for latent tuberculosis infection in adults 18 years and older who are at increased risk for infection (B grade recommendation). At-risk populations include persons who were born in or are former residents of countries with increased tuberculosis prevalence, and persons who live in or have lived in high-risk settings (eg, homeless shelters and correctional facilities).

A study in Vietnam, where the prevalence of TB is high, randomized clusters of communities to active screening or usual care with passive case detection. After 4 years, the prevalence of TB was significantly lower in the active screening communities (126 vs 226 cases per 100,000 persons, p < .0001).
QFT-G, which is a whole blood test, or TST can be used for screening. QFT-G can be used in place of (and not in addition to) the TST.
An advantage of QFT-G over TST is higher specificity in patients with a history of BCG vaccination or exposure to nontuberculous mycobacteria, and it also requires only one patient visit.
There are limited data on the use of QFT-G in young children, especially younger than 5 years, immunocompromised patients, and among patients recently exposed to M. tuberculosis.
Patients that screen positive with either test should be evaluated for TB disease. At minimum a CXR should be obtained before latent TB infection is diagnosed.
The BCG vaccine prevents serious forms of TB in children. It has not been proved to prevent pulmonary TB in adolescents and adults.
The BCG vaccine is not routinely used in the United States.
The decision to vaccinate should be made in consultation with local TB control programs.

In a 2017 Cochrane review, among HIV-positive children not taking ART, isoniazid was found to reduce the occurrance of active TB by 69%. Among HIV-positive children taking ART, no benefit or harm of isoniazid was identified.

A network meta-analysis of preventive regimens in persons living with HIV found that rifamycin containing regimens were safer and at least as effective as isoniazid regimens for preventing TB and death.
Suspect TB in a patient with prolonged cough, especially if accompanied by hemoptysis, fever, chills, sweats, and weight loss. C
If a screen for TB is positive, the patient needs at least a chest X-ray for evaluation. C
If pulmonary TB is suspected, obtain 3 induced sputums. C
For extrapulmonary disease, try to obtain a culture from the site of presumed infection. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Abscess with fluid level on X-ray

list.listitem: Suspect TB in a patient with prolonged cough, especially if accompanied by hemoptysis, fever, chills, sweats, and weight loss. Individual signs and symptoms are of limited value, although cough is fairly sensitive and night sweats and weight loss are fairly specific.

Initial assessment of a patient suspected to have active TB begins with a complete medical history that should include history of TB exposure, infection, or disease; history of BCG vaccination, sociodemographic factor (eg, country of origin, race or ethnicity, occupation); and medical conditions that increase the risk of TB such as HIV, diabetes mellitus, silicosis, or immunosuppressive therapy.
In pulmonary TB physical findings can vary from a normal lung exam to rales heard in the area of involvement.
Patients with extrapulmonary TB can present with varied physical findings, including painless lymphadenopathy, pain and swelling of the involved joint, meningeal signs, or focal neurologic findings.

NICE guidelines recommend testing all household contacts age 5 years and older of people with active TB. Begin with a Mantoux test, and if positive order an interferon-gamma test (IGT) to confirm the diagnosis.

CXR is sensitive but nonspecific for diagnosing TB; therefore the diagnosis cannot be established by radiography alone. The radiograph may be used to rule out pulmonary TB in asymptomatic patients with a positive TST or QFT-G.

AFB smear is the easiest and quickest procedure. But it permits only a presumptive diagnosis, since the AFB in the smear may not be M. tuberculosis. The predictive value of an AFB smear varies based on the pretest probability of TB. The AFB smear is most helpful in high-risk patients to rule-in disease, respectively. A negative smear does not rule out the diagnosis of TB.
Culture of M. tuberculosis confirms the diagnosis. Sensitivity of the culture is 80% to 85%, with a specificity of approximately 98%.
Nucleic amplification assay provides rapid confirmation of infection by M. tuberculosis with results in less than 48 hours from collection of specimen.
Genotyping of M. tuberculosis is used in the detection and control of outbreaks.

A cluster randomized trial in Uganda found that a program of on-site molecular testing for tuberculosis, guided restructuring of clinic workflows, and monthly feedback of quality metrics increased the number of patients diagnosed and treated for tuberculosis compared with smears and referral if abnormal (aRR 1.9, 95% CI 1.4 - 2.6).

T-cell based blood tests (ELISpot-Plus) have recently been compared to both 15 and 10 mm TST for the identification of culture-confirmed and highly probable TB. The sensitivity of the ELISpot-Plus was 83% to 89%. Patients with a negative TST and ELISpot-Plus had a very low probability of TB (LR −0.02).

A rapid test based on a PCR assay, called Xpert MTB/RIF, was found to be highly sensitive (97.6%) and specific (99.2%) for drug-resistant TB in a study of 1462 patients from Asia, Africa, and South America.

A systematic review identified 19 studies with 5855 samples comparing the Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra tests for tuberculosis. The latter was significantly more sensitive (84% vs 69%) and only slightly less specific (97% vs 99%). The positive and negative likelihood ratios for the Ultra test are 27 and 0.16 respectively.

In patients with pleural effusion, pleural fluid culture alone is very specific but insensitive (25%). Pleural biopsy along with culture and histology is recommended if TB is suspected in a patient with pleural effusion.
In the diagnosis of tuberculosis pleurisy, the TNF-α assay has a sensitivity and specificity of 80% and 85%, and the area under the curve (AUC) is 0.89.

The Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra molecular test was evaluated in samples from 317 persons with suspected pleural TB. It was 44% sensitive and 100% specific (LR+ 44, LR- 0.56) compared to a composite reference standard incorporating clinical, laboratory, histopathologic, and radiologic data at 12 month follow-up.

A clinical decision rule has been developed and prospectively validated to identify which inpatients need isolation for suspected pulmonary TB. It uses presence or absence of fever, respiratory symptoms, PPD test, and risk factors for TB.
A second rule was validated in a group of patients with a high prevalence of HIV disease and included CD4 counts.
In patients suspected of having pulmonary TB, CXRs should be obtained and 3 sputum samples collected on different days and examined for acid-fast bacillus smear and cultured for M. tuberculosis.
Spot sputum specimens are probably equivalent to early morning specimens in terms of diagnostic accuracy.

Samples of tissue or fluid should be obtained from the suspected site of infection and sent for acid-fast bacillus smear and culture when extrapulmonary TB is suspected. PCR can be done on specimens to hasten the diagnosis.
Drug susceptibility should be performed on initial isolates from all patients.
For latent TB, one of three 3-4 month regimens is recommended by CDC.A
For active TB, the initiation phase is 4 drugs for 2 months and the continuation phase is 2 drugs for 4 to 6 months. B
Patients at high risk for relapse should have the continuation phase for 7 months. B
Children with non-severe symptomatic TB can use a 4 month regimen of standard fixed dose anti-tubercular drugs. B

CDC guidelines recommend one of three 3 to 4 month regimens over older 6 to 9 month regimens for latent TB.
3 months of isoniazid (INH) plus rifapentine given once weekly (3HP). INH dose is 15 mg/kg in adults and children 12 and older, rounded to nearest 50 or 100 mg and with a maximum dose of 900 mg. For rifapentine, dose in adults and children 12 and older is weight based: 10-14 kg = 300 mg, 14.1-25 kg = 450 mg, 25.1-32 kg = 600 mg, 32.1-49.9 kg = 750 mg, and >= 50 kg = 900 mg maximum dose. For children 2 to 11 years, INH is 25 mg/kg and RPT is as above based on weight 4 months of daily rifampin (4R). CDC provides a checklist for monitoring adherence here. Dose of rifampin is 10 mg/kg for adults, 15-20 mg/kg for children, with a maximum dose of 600 mg daily. 3 months of daily isoniazid plus rifampin (3HR). CDC provides a checklist for monitoring adherence here. In adults, INH dose is 5 mg/kg with a maximum of 300 mg and for rifampin is 10 mg/kg with a 600 mg maximum. In children, INH dose is 10-20 mg/kg with a 300 mg maximum, and for rifampin is 15-20 mg/kg with a 600 mg maximum

In patients with HIV who have either latent TB or who are at high risk of acquiring TB, 1-month course of rifapentine plus isoniazid has been shown to be noninferior to a 9-month course of isoniazid in preventing TB infections and in preventing TB death.

The 2016 IDSA guidelines recommend the following regimens for pulmonary TB caused by drug susceptible organisms: Preferred regimen: Isoniazid (INH) + rifampin (RIF) + pyrazinamide (PZA) + ethambutol (EMB): 7 doses/week for 8 weeks or 5 doses/week for 8 weeks, followed by INH + RIF 7 doses/week for 18 weeks or 5 doses/week for 18 weeks. INH + RIF + PZA + EMB: 7 doses/week for 8 weeks or 5 doses/week for 8 weeks, followed by INH + RIF 3 times weekly for 18 weeks INH + RIF + PZA + EMB: 3 times weekly for 8 weeks, then INH + RIF 3 times weekly for 18 weeks INH+ RIF + PZA + EMB: 7 doses/week for 14 doses then twice weekly for 12 doses, followed by INH + RIF twice weekly for 18 weeks
In a randomized trial of 1204 children in Africa or India with symptomatic, non-severe, smear negative, drug susceptible TB, 4 months of standard anti-tubercular therapy was non-inferior to 6 months.

A study randomized 674 participants with rifampin susceptible TB to standard therapy (rifampin + isoniazid for 24 weeks with pyrazinamide and ethambutol during the first 8 weeks) or to one of 4 groups with different initial regimens given for 8 weeks followed by extended treatment if clinical disease persisted, post-treatment monitoring, and retreatment of any relapses. The group receiving 8 weeks of bedaquiline + linezolid was non-inferior to standard therapy (adjusted difference 0.8%, 95% CI -3.4 to 5.1%).
The added value of fluoroquinolones for treating tuberculosis is uncertain (5 small trials of low or very low quality) and is the focus of several ongoing clinical trials.

A regimen of intensified antituberculosis therapy (a 9-month regimen which included rifamin15 mg/kg/d and levofloxacin 20 mg/kg/d) was not associated with improved survival rates compared to the standard 9-month regimen which included rifampin 10 mg/kg/d).

In one, an RCT identified 2343 persons with pulmonary tuberculosis not resistant to isoniazid, rifampin, or fluoroquinolones and randomized them to 6 months of rifampin + isoniazid + pyrazinamide + ethambutol (standard regimen), the same regimen with rifapentine substituted for rifampin, or 4 months of rifapentine + isoniazid + pyrazinamide + moxifloxacin. The moxifloxacin based regimen was non-inferior to the standard regimen.

A study randomized 754 persons with rifampin resistant but fluoroquinolone susceptible TB to one of five 9-month oral regimens or standard therapy. The regimen found to be most effective was the combination of bedaquiline, linezolid, levofloxacin, and pyrazinamide (9.8% absolute improvement in favorable outcome, 95% CI 0.9 to 18.7%).

A study of 301 patients with rifampin resistant TB randomized them to usual care or the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid and moxifloxacin (BPaLM) for 24 weeks. Fewer patients in the BPaLM group had an outcome event of death, otreatment failure or discontinuation, loss to follow-up or recurrence (11% vs 48%, p < .01, NNT = 3).There were also fewer adverse events in the BPaLM group.
Multiply drug-resistant TB (MDRTB) and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDRTB) require a consult with an infectious disease specialist.
A small open label single arm trial found a favorable response in 98 of 109 patients with highly drug resistant TB given the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid for 26 weeks.
For patients with meningitis or pericarditis secondary to TB, corticosteroids should be used to improve outcomes.

A 2016 Cochrane review concluded that there was high quality evidence that corticosteroids in the treatment of tuberculous meningitis reduce the risk of death by 25% two months to two years after treament.

In people not infected with HIV who have tuberculous pericarditis, corticosteroids reduce the risk of mortality by 20% and the risk of pericardiocentesis by 15%. In people living with HIV and on retroviral agents, corticosteroids reduce the risk of constriction by 45%.
Patients with MDRTB may benefit from resection of cavitary or badly damaged lung tissue.

A Cochrane review concluded that there is no evidence that surgery improves outcomes when added to medications for patients with TB of the spine (Pott's disease). There were only two trials with 331 patients conducted in the 1970s and 80s, with no differences seen between groups for any outcome measure. Surgery may still be appropriate for selected patients, but this would be based on the surgeon's judgment of the likelihood of deterioration or collapse of the affected vertebrae.
Open surgical drainage reduces the risk of repeat periocardiocentesis by 77% but has little effect on other outcomes.
Direct observation therapy (DOT) should be considered for high-risk patients, especially those who are likely to present a transmission risk or to have problems with adherence to medications.
If given under direct observation, the "daily" dosing therapy may be given only 5 days a week.

However a recent Cochrane review concluded that there was no significant difference between DOT (observation by health workers, family members or community members) and self-administration in terms of cure, and called into question this practice "...until we better understand the situations in which it may be beneficial".

A systematic review that included 12 RCTs of nutritional supplements for patients being treated for active TB found some evidence that high energy supplements and zinc-based combinations of micronutrients lead to increases in body weight.

Counseling by nurses via the telephone or home visits increased adherence to therapy for latent TB from 65% to ~95%, and both of these interventions were superior to counseling by physicians at the TB clinic. No trials exist that examine the influence of counseling for the completion of treatment for active TB.

Material incentives to improve adherence, such as cash or vouchers, was studied in 11 trials found by a Cochrane review. These incentives appear to improve return for reading a TB test and clinic re-attendance, and may improve long-term adherence.

In a randomized controlled study, vitamin D 50,000 IU (three times weekly for 8 weeks and then every other week for 8 weeks) corrected vitamin D deficiency but had no effect on the rate of sputum mycobacterium tuberculosis clearance over 16 weeks.

3573 adults with a positive interferon-γ release assay but no symptoms or evidence of active disease were randomized to recieve a vaccine against MTB (M72/AS01E) or a placebo vaccine. After 36 months the incidence of symptomatic TB was 0.3 v 0.6 cases per 100 person-years (NNT = 333 over 3 years), the frequencies of serious adverse events were similar between the two groups.
Patients with MDRTB and XDRTB should be referred to an infectious disease specialist.
By law, all cases of active TB must be reported to the local health department.
Patients with active TB should be placed in negative pressure rooms.
In patients with HIV and latent TB, the rate of acquiring active TB is 5% to 10% a year. In patients with latent TB and no HIV infection, 10% will go on to develop active TB during their lifetime. B

Patients with active TB should have induced sputum at the end of the initial 2 months of therapy. If the TB is not cleared at 2 months, repeat the cultures in addition to therapy. Positive sputum cultures at 2 months and cavitary pulmonary lesions are associated with a relapse. B

In a randomized clinical trial 850 patients with advanced AIDS (mean CD4 count 18 cells per uL), 424 patients received empirical tuberculosis therapy and 426 recieved isoniazid (INH) preventive therapy prior to initiating anti-retroviral therapy. Patients with confirmed TB were excluded. At week 24 there were no between group differences in mortality (~5% in each group) or in signs or symptoms or laboratory abnormalities; this support INH preventive therapy in patients with advanced AIDS who are initiating antiretroviral therapy.

In pregnancy with moderate suspicion of TB use INH, RIF, and EMB for 9 months. These drugs cross the placenta, but no teratogenic effects have been shown. Consider consultation with an infectious disease specialist and with an obstetrician specializing in high-risk pregnancies.
Breast-feeding should not be discouraged. Only small concentrations occur in the breast milk and do not produce toxic effects.
For latent TB, treat children with INH 10 to 15 mg/kg (300 mg maximum dose) daily for 6 months.

WHO guidelines (2022) recommend Xpert MTB/RIF as the initial diagnostic test for TB and rifampicin-resistance detection in sputum, gastric aspirate, nasopharyngeal aspirate, and stool that in children with signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB.
In a randomized trial of 1204 children in Africa or India with symptomatic, non-severe, smear negative, drug susceptible TB, 4 months of standard anti-tubercular therapy was non-inferior to 6 months.
Updated WHO guidelines (2022) recommend 4 months of treatment using standard fixed dose anti-tuberculosis treatment (2HRZ(E)/2HR).
In a systematic review of retrials including 991 HIV-positive children (age <13) not taking ART, isoniazid reduced the number of children developing active TB by 69%, and death by 54%.
For active TB, treat children with INH 10 to 15 mg/kg (max 300 mg), RIF 10 to 20 mg/kg (max 600 mg), and PYZ 15 to 30 mg/kg (max 2 g) for 2 weeks to 2 months, and then 4 months of INH and RIF.
Avoid ethambutol in children, although it is an option in selected children at high risk for MDRTB.
Directly observed therapy should always be used for children.
A prospective cohort study of 149 children with multidrug resistant TB treated according to local standard of care resulted in definite or probable cure for 92%.

A systematic review and meta-analyisis of 46 cohort studies with 137,647 tuberculosis-exposed children, demonstrated that: 1) the two year cumullative risk of TB is 20%, 2) most of these cases are diagnosed within 90 days of exposure, and 2) the effectiveness of preventive therapy for the 2-year cumulative tuberculosis incidence was 63 to 91% compared to those not recieving preventive therapy after TB exposure.

feature.feature_body:
HIV-positive persons
Recent contacts of tuberculosis case patients
Recent immigrants from high-prevalence countries (within the last 5 years)
Injection drug users
Residents and employees of high-risk congregate settings (jails, nursing homes, health care facilities, homeless shelters)
Children and adolescents exposed to adults at high risk
Medically underserved, low-income population
Racial and ethnic minorities
Medical risk factors that increases the risk of disease if infection occurs: diabetes mellitus, silicosis, chronic renal failure, malignancy, weight loss of >10% of ideal body weight, gastrectomy, and jejunoileal bypass
Data from Screening for tuberculosis and tuberculosis infection in high-risk populations. Recommendations of the Advisory Council for the Elimination of Tuberculosis. MMWR Recomm Rep 1995;44(RR-11):19-34.
